This page covers exact U.S. occupation O*NET / SOC 17-2111.00, Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors: promote worksite or product safety using industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws, including industrial product safety engineers. Official scope: Promote worksite or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Includes industrial product safety engineers. O*NET core tasks include investigating industrial accidents, injuries, or occupational diseases to identify causes and prevention (importance 88); studying product safety levels (84); evaluating design safety (83); conducting or coordinating employee training in safety laws, hazardous-condition monitoring, and safety equipment use (82); maintaining and applying current policy, regulatory, and industrial-process knowledge (82); recommending procedures to detect, prevent, and eliminate physical, chemical, or other product hazards (82); reporting or reviewing accident investigation, facility inspection, or environmental test findings (81); assessing potential health hazards or damage from product misuse (81); evaluating adequacy of action correcting health-inspection violations (77); interpreting safety regulations for others concerned with industrial safety (74); reviewing new machinery or equipment construction plans and specifications against all safety requirements (73); helping prepare product-use and warning-label instructions (72); interviewing employers and employees about work environments and incidents (70); providing expert testimony in litigation (70); reviewing employee safety programs for adequacy (70); conducting or directing air-quality, noise, temperature, or radiation testing for compliance (70); advising organizations on health-related issues and necessary changes (69); developing industry product safety standards (65); liaising with external organizations such as fire departments, mutual-aid societies, and rescue teams for emergency response (65); planning and conducting industrial hygiene research (61); compiling, analyzing, and interpreting occupational disease and accident statistics (59); writing and revising safety regulations and codes (58); designing and building safety equipment (58); consulting medical professionals on health risks and management approaches (57); checking factory floors for strength to support heavy machinery (50). Additional tasks include inspecting facilities, machinery, or safety equipment to identify and correct hazards and ensure compliance, and installing or directing installation of machinery safety devices. Common titles include Health and Safety Specialist, Industrial Hygienist, Industrial Safety Engineer, Product Safety Engineer, Safety Engineer, System Safety Engineer, Product Safety Consultant, and Safety and Health Consultant. Wage, employment, and industry figures use this occupation's own scope as displayed by O*NET on 17-2111.00, without a higher- or parent-occupation label; 2024—2034 growth is 'Average (3% to 4%)'. Exercise | An entirely fictional workplace and product safety assessment package, for process practice only, representing no actual enterprise, site, product, incident, client, or data. Draft a plan covering: (1) how to structure hazard identification, risk assessment, and compliance review from a fictional workplace hazard list and product safety design description: hazard categories, exposure routes and affected populations; likelihood, severity, and priority; existing controls and applicable regulations and standards; corrective recommendations, responsibilities and deadlines; residual risks and review. Identify missing information: processes, equipment and materials, exposure monitoring and occupational limits, applicable regulatory and standard versions, intended use and misuse, and past accident and inspection records. (2) Design completion and review points for a fictional hazard, risk, and corrective-action tracking form: fields and units; hazards, areas, positions and populations; likelihood, severity and risk levels; control hierarchy and responsible persons; deadlines, verification and closure evidence; originals and traceable revisions. (3) Write a transferable assessment summary: scope and methods—hazards and risks—regulatory and standards compliance—corrective recommendations and priorities—residual risks and outstanding issues. (4) Record and retain assessment, monitoring, correction, training, and accident investigation records; distinguish disclosable information from controlled information or materials involving enterprises, employees, or personal information. (5) Pause, review, and report insufficient data or invalid assumptions, correction measures conflicting with regulations, accidents or exposures beyond assessment scope, and conclusions requiring statutory qualifications or exceeding job authority. Use public materials and simulated data, without real enterprise data or personally identifying information.

Direct answer | This page covers exact occupation O*NET 17-2111.00, Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors. Work categories: (I) Hazard identification and monitoring—inspect facilities, machinery, and safety equipment to identify and correct hazards; conduct or direct air-quality, noise, temperature, or radiation tests against safety laws; check factory floor strength for heavy machinery. (II) Risk assessment and compliance review—assess corrective actions for health-inspection violations, review machinery or equipment construction plans and specifications against safety requirements, and maintain current policy, regulatory, and process knowledge. (III) Corrective recommendations and standards—recommend detection, prevention, and elimination procedures for physical, chemical, or other product hazards, develop industry product safety standards, write and revise safety regulations and codes, and design and build safety equipment. (IV) Accident investigation and professional support—investigate industrial accidents, injuries, and occupational disease for causes and prevention, report or review investigation, inspection, and environmental-test findings, provide expert testimony, and consult medical professionals on health risks. (V) Product safety review—research safety levels, assess design safety and misuse hazards or damage, and help prepare use and warning-label instructions. (VI) Training and coordination—conduct or coordinate employee safety-law, hazard-monitoring, and equipment-use training; review employee safety programs; advise on health issues; and liaise with fire departments, mutual-aid societies, rescue teams, and others for emergencies. Work cycle: identification and monitoring—risk and compliance review—corrective advice and standards—investigation and professional support—product safety review—training, coordination, and review. This occupation is distinct from environmental compliance inspectors, fire-protection engineers, environmental engineers, environmental scientists, environmental protection technicians, occupational health specialists and technicians, industrial engineers, and safety management specialists. Its duties do not replace statutorily qualified organizations' accident, recall, or compliance decisions.

subject.name: Health and Safety Engineers
subject.summary: Health and safety engineers correspond to exact occupation O*NET / SOC 17-2111.00, Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors: promote worksite or product safety using knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws, including industrial product safety engineers. Core tasks include investigating industrial accidents and occupational diseases, evaluating product designs and misuse risks, conducting or directing air, noise, temperature, and radiation testing, evaluating corrective-action adequacy, reviewing machinery and equipment plans and specifications, and employee safety training. Common titles include Health and Safety Specialist, Industrial Hygienist, Industrial Safety Engineer, Product Safety Engineer, and Safety Engineer. Official scope: Promote worksite or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Includes industrial product safety engineers. Scope note: U.S. wages and employment use this occupation's own scope (17-2111.00) as presented by O*NET on 17-2111.00, without a parent-occupation label or substitution of neighboring figures. Projected 2024—2034 growth is 3% to 4%; O*NET assigns Job Zone Four (considerable preparation, SVP 7.0 to below 8.0). This page provides no occupational safety, product safety, industrial hygiene, medical, legal, or compliance advice.
